speechtext: And $3 wheat now.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Yes, $3 wheat now, but the domestic purchaser is not paying $3 per bushel for the wheat he purchases. The mills are paying $1.95 at Thunder Bay. Either we must take steps to subsidize our producers, if we want to achieve and maintain a healthy agricultural industry, or else the consumer must pay more. Immediately on assuming office, the government reduced the initial price of wheat. It removed the premium on the production of hogs, which was something in the order of $10 million. It unilaterally and indiscriminately destroyed the small dairy producers. The government received recommendations from the Royal Commission on the Price of Farm Machinery, but not one of those recommendations has been implemented.
Then we had a Prices and Incomes Commission that was another complete and total failure. It did nothing with respect to narrowing the gap. We had a Prime Minister who in December, 1970, said that inflation was licked. Mr. Speaker, it was licked then simply because there was a war on between the food chains, and also because the producers were getting very low returns for their produce.
What has happened to the cost of in-puts generally? Farm in-puts have risen from an index base of 100 in 1961 to 135.4 in 1971. Farm labour costs, based on 100 in 1961, have risen to 178.2. How has the farmer survived? He has survived simply by increasing his productive capacity. He has increased his productivity by 13 per cent per annum over the past two decades. Meanwhile, the cost of processing and distributing has increased about six times as rapidly as the return to the producer. This is manifested by the fact that in 1971, out of a total Canadian food bill of $7 billion, only 6 per cent of that went to the primary producer. This was a drop of 4 per cent since 1959. If you measure it in constant dollars, you would probably have to deduct a further 35 per cent from that figure. This

simply means that 94 per cent of the consumer's dollar is received by someone other than the primary producer. I suggest that this is ridiculous and must be corrected. If this inquiry is going to be totally objective it will bear this out, and place the welfare of the producer in its proper perspective.
I suggest that the whole inflationary cycle which is upon us at this time is something that the government has failed to correct. I believe that its policies and non-policies have helped to exacerbate the problems of inflation. I know that the food processors and those charged with the distributing of food products are getting the major brunt of the blame in this particular area, but I am sure that they, too, have had their problems with increased costs. This part of the food industry has, in fact experienced a very sharp increase in costs, increased basic costs of labour, of transportation, higher taxes, higher costs of urban land- these have all risen rapidly due to inflationary forces.
Other things which have contributed to higher food costs include an increase in the degree to which foods are processed. Canadians are buying more of their food products in more highly processed forms. There are very few products sold now in their natural, raw state. There is a great deal more prepackaging of foods. Then, there is the matter of increased shopping convenience. As mentioned by other hon. members, there are the huge outlays of money on great shopping malls and supermarkets. Someone must pay for those costs, Mr. Speaker. Who pays? The consumer pays.
I do not think too many members have touched on the matter of imports. A large portion of our food bill is for imported foods. This is something over which we really have very limited control. The prices of foods that we import have risen sharply. We are victimized by high transportation costs. Many of the products imported are of a seasonal variety. Then, there is the matter of tariffs, particularly tariffs on those items that are highly processed.
To put this thing into perspective, Mr. Speaker, I wish to give a few figures. In 1969, for the first time in the history of Canada, we imported $35 million more worth of agricultural products than we exported. That is a shame in a country such as Canada, with its expertise in agricultural production and its ability to produce. We are still importing $1.3 billion worth of agricultural products per annum. As I say, we really do not have too much control over the cost of those products. I suggest that in large part many of those products could be produced in Canada. Instead of discouraging the production of many of these agricultural products, I think we might do well to diversify our production to take in some of the items which we import. At the present time we are encouraging and paying farmers to leave the land and limit production. I believe this is an area that the Department of Agriculture could look at in a positive and rational manner. Many of the items we import we could produce quite effectively at home.
There is a great need for diversification in our agricultural industry. We would do well to promote a healthy, viable agriculture industry by encouraging more diversification. In short, I believe we must maximize our production and we must diversify our production. It is important



also that we take steps to bolster those sectors of our agriculture industry that from time to time may suffer depression. As we have experienced in previous years, if we get a recession in the wheat industry it tends to spread to the hog or livestock industry. This situation must be corrected by government action. I am suggesting here, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Agriculture should look very positively at protecting those sectors of agriculture which depend upon one another.
It seems that the government is bent on maintaining a cheap food policy, but if we are to have that we must have subsidies to the producer. There is no way that we can maintain an effective, healthy and viable agriculture industry unless there is a return for it and we cannot maintain the return unless we get it from someone. That is the decision that we must make. If we do not get it from the consumer, we must get it from the Treasury and that means some kind of subsidization for the producer. Increased labour costs, taxes, increased machinery costs and all the other inputs that producers have been confronted with cannot continue to rise without a corresponding increase in returns to the producer. If we have only an income comparable to the level of 1951, it is unlikely that agriculture can survive as a healthy productive industry.
Another area that needs consideration is that of transportation costs. There are great discrepancies between the rates in the east and the rates in the west, particularly in the area of processed agricultural products.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think the government should examine its own expenditures because they, too, have a very inflationary effect upon the production, distribution and processing of agricultural products. Above all, I think government should refrain from further interference, further regimentation and further regulation of the industry. We have seen much of that in the past four years. Some of the programs thrust upon farmers have been so embossed with red tape that they have been difficult to implement. Less government interference would be welcome. I hope that the committee will take a very constructive approach to the examination of food prices, and I hope it will keep the welfare of the producer in its proper perspective.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE TO $75,000 IN MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF LOANS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Small Businesses Loans Act to increase the maximal amount of a loan thereunder to $75,000.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I discussed this notice of motion before bringing it before the House. We find no real objection to some of the items spelled out in the Small Businesses Loans Act. It first came into force 11 or 12 years ago, in 1961, for an initial period of three years and was subsequently amended to offer a wide range of opportunities for businessmen who wished to borrow money to improve their businesses. They could use such money for the purchase of fixed or movable equipment, the construction of premises or the improvement or modernization of premises. The act defines a small business as one with gross revenues not exceeding $500,000. From this point on, my colleagues and I begin to differ with the act. We feel that the maximum amount of $25,000 for a loan, as at present specified, in no way reflects what is reasonable for businessmen in Canada today. If one were in the construction business, $25,000 would not begin to buy some pieces of equipment; if one were in the manufacturing business, one could not buy

much by way of raw materials for $25,000. In the wholesale business, $25,000 would not even buy you a decent stock of cigarettes, never mind anything else. In the transport business, you could not buy one truck of reasonable size for $25,000.
In my maiden speech in the House, I made a point of saying what I thought of the Industrial Development Bank. Supposedly, it is a court of last resort for businessmen. It operates in the high risk area but, at present, definitely does not fill the needs of businessmen. The bank is far too protective and asks for far too much by way of security for the types of loans it makes. I repeat, its interest rates are usurious, to say the least.
The Small Businesses Loans Act was meant to help smaller businesses, because it was thought smaller loans would be an asset to businessmen of the type I have described. We contend, however, that even in that particular area the Small Businesses Loans Act fails. On looking at the statistics relating to the Small Businesses Loans Act for 1971, we find that were 2,129 loans, amounting to $22.3 million, for an average of $10,460 per loan. Of those, service businesses accounted for 37 per cent, retail for 22 per cent, construction for 14 per cent and manufacturing for 13 per cent. These are exactly the types of businesses that the Industrial Development Bank pretends to service.
We do not quarrel with the percentage of loans made in various provinces. On reading the report one will find that they are spread pretty well across the provinces in proportion to population. The banks which actually administer the loans seem, if one considers their size in relation to that of the community, to grant a reasonable percentage of such loans. We are suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that if 40 per cent of the maximum is the average criterion in granting loans, the average loans being for $10,500, or approximately 40 per cent of $25,000 allowed as a maximum, that by increasing the maximum to $75,000 loans of a reasonable size could be granted to the business community.
In 1961, the average loan was in the order of $8,500. The increase of $2,000 in ten year to $10,500 in no way, shape or form reflects increases in costs that must be met. I suggest that if one considers true dollar purchasing power, the size of loans has actually gone down, not increased. I suggest that this does not reflect the sort of activity that one might expect from legislation first passed in 1961 and now 12 years old. We suggest that as more people become aware of the existence of this loan program, the size of loans granted would have increased as well.
I know that motions of the type I am presenting are usually talked out by members on the government side. I suggest this to hon. members on the government side: Are there not in their communities, perhaps, businessmen who might need some extra money for their businesses, whether those be manufacturing, retail or service businesses? Are there not businessmen in their ridings who want extra help in putting their businesses together? Or is it that members on the government side do not care whether businessmen in their areas want or need extra help with their businesses?
Members on the opposition side of the House have stated very carefully how they feel about small business and how we ought to proceed if we are to help small
January 22, 1973

business which is the life blood of the Canadian economy. My colleagues and I think that the motion before the House covers the situation pretty well. This is not an attempt to give money away. The motion speaks of loans to businessmen. We are not asking for something for nothing. If indeed this notice of motion is talked out by my colleagues on the other side of the House, then I ask them to promise us that there will be action of some sort by way of a government bill that will do the same job as the motion would seek to do and increase in a reasonable way the amounts of business loans that are available to small businessmen.
If I may repeat, Mr. Speaker, the Industrial Development Bank is not doing its job. The Small Businesses Loans Act could be a tremendous support to small businessmen if they were allowed to borrow reasonable amounts of money. We suggest that the new maximum should be $75,000.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the subject of small business because I believe it is an area of substantial strength in our economy and it offers perhaps the greatest potential for growth. I, therefore, thank the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) for bringing this matter to our attention. This is also an area in which I have had some experience, going through the incubation stage of a business, struggling through growth and seeing it mature. All of these are difficult stages, as only one who has been through them can really understand.
First, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) said in the throne speech debate, some 60 per cent of all employed Canadians work for enterprises which can be categorized as small businesses. They account for some 30 per cent of our gross national product or $31 billion in some 350,000 enterprises.
Second, and quite important, all large businesses were once small. It is too bad the hon. member who raised this motion said that this side of the House is not interested in this subject. His few words represented a peanut type approach that did not amount to anything more than the other two suggestions. I heard from the oppostion about
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger).]
small-thinking programs. The hon. member has left the chamber. I question whether he is really interested in small business.
Third, most small businesses are Canadian owned. Their growth offers real hope of Canadian ownership of our economy in the future in a non-restrictive, non-punitive and very positive way. In addition, small businesses offer opportunity and challenge for Canadian entrepreneurs, and help sustain bigger business both as a customer and supplier. This type of business helps small communities and contributes to the alleviation of regional economic disparities, as well as assuring competition in both products and prices. Such businesses are generally labour intensive and usually quite efficient. Very importantly, they are highly innovative, flexible and rapidly responsive to change or market conditions. Because they are less capital intensive, they can respond quickly to the stimulus of invested capital.
The question is, how can government help small business? I have had several thoughts based on my own experience, but in order to get a broader approach I have been meeting and working with a diverse group from the private sector over the past several months. In this process we met with the present and former ministers of industry, trade and commerce as well as their senior officials, and we also went to Washington to discuss the approach of the small businesses administration in the United States where we were warmly received by its chief, Mr. Tom Kleppe, and his advisers.
There is no one simple solution. It requires a multifaceted approach to respond to a variety of situations. In developing such a response I am indebted to a group that includes management consultants, venture capitalists, bankers, men who operate their own small and mediumsized businesses, and men such as John Bullock and John Earle of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. While I do not suggest that all of my views are theirs, their input has been invaluable, as has been the work of OECD and experience in other developed nations. In most cases, the cost to government is minimal. Indeed, when one considers the return to the economy and treasury, the gains are substantial.
The Small Business Administration in the United States operates on the principle of no giveaways. There are loans and guarantees, but they calculate that through proper programs they have created one new job for each $1,500, not in costs but in loans or guarantees. The direct losses are minimal, and if we are really to move in this direction, we should be prepared for an acceptable loss ratio. In the United States, the programs with the greatest losses have losses under 5 per cent, and most are well under this.
To really be of help, we have to make a commitment to be seriously and energetically interested in small business, as the hon. member for Hastings urges. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has taken a very significant step in announcing one stop service when dealing with government and, very importantly, decentralizing this service across the country, as the parliamentary secretary has just said. There is nothing more frustrating to the small businessman, usually wearing a
January 22, 1973

number of management hats, than to come to Ottawa trying to find the right man in the right department and leaving with a sheaf of applications in his hand. If he has time to fill them out, he does not have time to wait until they filter through the bureaucracy. When any legislation is passed, the interests of the small businessman and the impact of that legislation upon him must be considered.
Government itself must back up its commitment by directing an appropriate percentage of all government purchases to qualified small business. In addition, it must insist that all government business given to major contractors or vendors carries the stipulation that a given percentage of subcontracts or purchases come from small business. The Americans call this their "set aside program" and it has resulted in surprising new sources and savings as a consequence of shopping around for small suppliers, rather than taking the path of least resistance and going only to the other "big boys" they know so well. The impetus that this has given to smaller enterprises and the economy as a whole is incalculable.
There should also be national and regional advisory groups to government, largely comprised of small business representatives. They can offer valuable guidance to government, help tailor programs more closely to their needs, co-ordinate government efforts in the private sector, and generally work in partnership rather than in frustration or with a lesser impact than the potential of many excellent government programs.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business proposes an entrepreneurial council to carry out many of these roles and to actively seek out Canadian manufacturers to match many imports of products or components to existing or potential Canadian manufacturing facilities, establishing continuing mechanisms to maintain this coordination. Of vital importance-I am sorry that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has left the chamber-is revising our sales tax regulations so they work to the benefit of the Canadian manufacturers as opposed to imported goods, as is often the case today.
The management programs already functioning and being expanded substantially are of considerable value, as proper management techniques are critical, often more critical than capital, to many small businessmen whose drive, expertise and experience can often be dissipated by inadequate management procedures.
But capital is also vitally important. The IDB has been eminently successful in responding to much of this need and I welcome the minister's announcement that this highly successful, and increasingly aggressive agency is reviewing its role so that its experience and expertise can be put to even greater use. I share the hon. member's frustrations regarding the IDB, though I thought he was a little unfair in his remarks in the throne speech debate. I felt that way when I came here and, after going into the matter further, I am certainly satisfied that it deserves a better look. Perhaps things will improve as a result of my speech.
The Small Businesses Loans Act that this motion is specifically directed to should also be amended substantially to make it more relevant to today's realities. This must mean considerably higher limits. The hon. member suggested $75,000; I prepared these remarks for the
Small Business Loans
throne speech debate and was unable to get on, but I suggest a minimum of $100,000 and interest rates that will be competitive in attracting the necessary capital. The banks just will not go along with low rates, simply because they are unrealistic.
However-and this goes to the essence of the point contained in the hon. member's motion-this may not be necessary in view of the announcement of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce of a greatly expanded role for the general adjustment assistance plan, called GAAP. This, when available to all or to most businesses, may be even more effective, particularly when it already has its own administration and board. A similar program under the small businesses administration in the United States is its major program with $1J billion guaranteed last year, which amount is to be increased to $1.5 billion this year, and with a loss ratio of some 3.5 per cent. I think in crowing about high risk areas with a satisfactory profit picture we should also be prepared to accept a satisfactory loss ratio.
Another very interesting program of the small businesses administration of the United States is the small business investment company program. This program borrows money from conventional money markets, taking advantage of vast capital pools from insurance companies, mutual funds, foundation and pension funds, the latter a particularly fast growing source in Canada due to the requirement of our tax reform that 90 per cent of the assets of such bodies be invested in Canada. This is a good investment at a low but attractive rate due to the government guarantee. This money, then, is loaned to the SBIC, the Small Business Investment Corporation, at a rate of 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent additional, the current rate running at approximately 6.9 per cent. So it is not actually government money; it is merely the use of government guarantees.
The SBIC is a licensed venture capital company with good management experience and a good track record. For every dollar the SBIC invests of its own, the small businesses administration will lend up to $3. This is longer term money, lent over 15 to 20 years.
Since the term "venture capital" implies risk taking, this company usually gets involved in high potential and relatively high risk ventures, the kind which, when they do pay off, really add to the economy significantly. The losers generally show up early and the winners often take a long time coming. You have to hang tough with this sort of thing and be prepared for some losses in the early days. This fact has scared off the conventional money lenders, but there is a commitment to the program from good venture capital investors. I do not say that all of them are good, but many are.
In its initial stages, this program in the United States got off to a bad start as it was too loosely structured and monitored, if it was monitored at all. The number of licensed SBIC's in the United States has been reduced from 800 to some 300 effective organizations, and more consistently positive results are emerging. The speculator, the inefficient, the inexperienced have all been weeded out, and some of the vultures, too. They have tended to get in on the act and some very undesirable things happened, but as I say they have now been monitored out, largely as

a result of the action of Tom Kleppe, the administrator over the last 18 months or so who has done a magnificent job. The whole thing has been a stimulating experience.
We are in a position to benefit from this experience and to adapt it to our own needs and know-how. Regionally established SBIC's in Canada could have an invigorating effect particularly on the economies of our disadvantaged regions and provide very real opportunities.
I suspect that in many parts of the country where their economies are based on fishing, forestry and other resource industries there is much talent but limited opportunity. Who could better see the opportunities, know the people and the markets than the businessmen in those areas, men who have a feel for the region and its potential who with adequate resources plus their skill and instinct can help the local people in new enterprises, with their attendant jobs, to get off the ground much faster and more economically than government agencies at all levels no matter how skilled and dedicated are our public servants. After all, local businessmen have their own money at stake too.
Without delaying action in the area of small business, I believe we should try to learn a great deal more about small business. It is surprising how little really reliable information on small businesses is available in this country. I would think that in more tranquil political times we could have the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs conduct a study in this area. In addition to this, however, an organization such as the conference board in Canada, under the direction of one of Canada's most distinguised economists, Dr. Arthur Smith, could and should undertake such a task. This could be done by a similar group with the professional expertise and research facilities necessary.
May I say that in thinking of business we have been inclined to place emphasis on manufacturing and exporting, both vital, but I believe we should give parallel attention to the rapidly growing and labour-intensive service sector. Some 40 per cent of our gross national product comes from that sector today, without counting government at all levels which would bring it up to about 70 per cent. With growing automation and sophistication and increasing leisure time, it will afford our greatest areas of opportunity, most of which cannot be replaced by imports. It can however, be foreign-owned. Indeed, the chances are that it will be if we do not nurture and encourage it in a Canadian context.
In this respect, I am pleased with the announcement by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) of increased assistance to the tourist industry; but that is only part of it. This is only highlighting a subject which deserves the very high priority it now appears to be getting from this government and I look forward to greater elaboration of the policies already announced and those yet to come in the budget. This priority attention must be sustained. In this respect I am happy to note the administrative changes in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, with two assistant deputy ministers so that one can concentrate on domestic industry and one on exports. This might bring a

closer identity in each of these areas which existed before the department of industry and the department of trade and commerce were merged.
Frankly, I believe that the merger was a mistake because it reduced the political contact between the business community and the cabinet. Though the former minister and the present minister are men of outstanding ability and capacity, their concerns are about exports and trade agreements and it is very difficult for them to spread themselves so thinly. I think there are other able ministers in the cabinet today who are perhaps underutilized and who could go into the departments in an associate capacity and serve in the area of liaison with the private sector. This is something that would give added assistance to the small business area. The important thing is tne recognition of small business, its importance to the economy and its potential for future development in a Canadian context. We must commit ourselves to its success and give Canadian businessmen and women of imagination and enterprise a fighting chance of survival over what are frequently overwhelming odds.
Having been through this, Mr. Speaker, there are three stages in starting a business. The first is that you must have the guts to leave your job and start. Nobody really thinks you can make it except you. You go to the bank for a little help but the banker thinks you are crazy and should have stayed at your own job. You are too involved and confused to worry about reports, returns on investment, deliveries and so forth.
Next is the adolescent stage when you are determined you can be successful. You may have a couple of people helping you, such as a girl in the office and a shipper in the shipping room, or another salesman. But you need extra capital, perhaps in the range of $50,000. The banks are not interested in talking to you; they are interested in sales projections, cash flows and such things. If you are fortunate enough to obtain the money, not that you really need it to stay in business, then you have the confidence that it gives you to invest in new people, new projects and new schemes.
Then we come to the third stage, not the final stage, which I have always called the menopause stage in business when you really develop and become a success. You may have reached the limits of your own managerial capacity although you may have had a great deal of difficulty. You are balancing your receivables against your payables and deliveries, and you have the bank manager on your back and your wife on your back because she wonders why you are working 60 or 80 hours a week. This gets pretty trying.
Then somebody in a similar business comes along, perhaps from Milwaukee or somewhere else and says, "Barney, how is business?" You say it is great, but you haven't the necessary cash flow and nobody is interested in giving you the money. He then says, "You don't have to worry any more; I can give you the $250,000", $500,000 or whatever it is. "We will give you a salary of $25,000," $35,000 or $50,000 "a year under a ten-year contract and 10 per cent of the profits". You haven't drawn a nickel in profit from your business in all this time and you think you are nuts not to accept the man's offer. As a result, the business is lost to Canada. The entrepreneur has made a good capital

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE TO $75,000 IN MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF LOANS
speechtext:
It is an honour for me to speak in support of the motion presented by the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis). The motion asks that the government consider increasing the maximum loan available under the Small Businesses Loans Act from $25,000 to $75,000.
I am an operator of a small business and I know all the frustrations that face small businessmen. I also know what this increase will mean to thousands of people classed as small businessmen in Canada today. When you examine the sources of funds available to the small businessman you see the dilemma he faces. The chartered banks are in the retail credit business, automobile financing, residential mortgages and numerous other fields heretofore occupied by others. Each time the chartered banks enter a new field, the amount of money available to the small businessman diminishes. They will tell you this is not the case, but when one applies for a loan that is what one learns really is the situation.
For a moment let us consider the small businessman. He is a merchant, a small manufacturer, an agent or one of the thousands engaged in that broad category called the service industry. We have heard from previous speakers that these people are the largest employers in Canada. Collectively they have the capacity to significantly aid in the reduction of unemployment in Canada. Small businesses rarely lay off their staff during economic slowdowns. They are flexible and can expand rapidly when required. They are the stabilizing force in most communities and collectively import tremendous stability to the economy of Canada.
The single most pressing need is for funds to update or expand their businesses. To remain healthy they must keep abreast of the market in which they compete. Today's small businesses are the large businesses of tomorrow. They are almost 100 per cent Canadian-owned and operated. We should keep that in mind. We are discussing at some levels in this House foreign ownership policy and a screening board. Here we have Canadian-owned and operated businesses in need of assistance in the form of repayable loans at reasonable rates of interest. They do not seek grants or subsidies or floor prices. They only seek adequate funds to operate their businesses as only they know best.
Various other federal and provincial agencies do not normally have programs for businesses of the type I have mentioned. Probably the most significant move we can make is to help them by increasing the ceiling on loans available under the Small Businesses Loans Act from $25,000 to $75,000. I urge hon. members to adopt this motion.
I do not wish to speak very much about the IDB. I have done business with that agency and I know the situation. I understand the frustration in this area and the situation in respect of the interest rate at 11 per cent or 12 per cent, which is 3 per cent above that of the commercial banks whose rate was 9 per cent. I know what the IDB is all about. I can tell hon. members that the average small businessman does not want to deal with any government agency because of the red tape involved.

January 22, 1973

The businessmen with whom I am associated are probably the last persons who would go to a government agency for advice in respect of their businesses. When I hear about the offices which are to be opened for the purpose of advising businessmen, I shudder. I shall not say much about the CASE program because I am not very well informed in respect of it. However, as a practising businessman the last thing I would do would be to go to a government agency and ask for advice on how to run my business.
I think the most useful thing we can do to help the small businessman is to increase the ceiling on loans under this program from $25,000 to $75,000. I therefore urge hon. members to adopt this motion.

Tonight, we are debating a notice of motion for raising to $75,000 the ceiling on loans available to small businesses. Mr. Speaker, I think that we should consider the problem in a much more comprehensive and general manner. At present, there are two ways of obtaining credit from the federal government for the small and medium businesses. First, there are the small business loans granted through the Industrial Development Bank. In my opinion, the hon. member for Hasting (Mr. Ellis) has well covered the matter of increasing the maximum amount of such loans, but I believe he ignored very important factors.
As concerns the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), he insisted mainly on the important role being assumed by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce concerning assistance bo businesses in general, and I believe that he too has discussed that role quite well, though very briefly.
The hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) no doubt had worked somewhat harder on the speech he was to deliver in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, but I believe that he dealt here with almost all the important points to be considered.
The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) has underlined some weaknesses to be found in the current administration of such legislation.
Although I have been parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance for a few weeks only perhaps I might put forward some ideas on the subject.
In my opinion, the most important thing that we should consider is a complete revision of both programs. If we could find some means of combining and integrating those two programs into a single one perhaps we might partly solve our problem in view of the fact that in our modern world of 1973 it is very difficult to distinguish small businesses from medium-size businesses. I think that a turnover of $500,000 does not mean anything today nor does a maximum loan of $75,000.
The Speech from the Throne stated that great importance should be given to the medium-size businesses and the people who operate them. And what makes me rather optimistic in this connection is that the medium-size or small business is the most important source of employment for people 45 or over and most often not unskilled.
Having worked for a business firm I know from experience that the facts mentioned by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth are true to a certain extent. It is quite difficult for a medium-size business to have dealings with a government agency. In my opinion, this is not a flaw in the legislation but rather a gap in administration and personnel which in some cases should be filled.

Before the debate was interrupted at five o'clock I was answering a few of the points that had been made by the party to my right, and now I would like to make one or two further points. Some opposition was expressed to the point of view put forward by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that food in this country was a bargain for Canadians. It certainly is so far as the farmer-producer is concerned. Someone said there would be long, cold months ahead for those on fixed incomes. This will depend upon how high or how low the incomes are fixed. For those who are comparatively well-to-do it is not a great problem. For those who are not in that position it creates an almost insurmountable problem. I hope that as a result of this proposed investigation we will arrive at some procedures or proposals to make food more readily available to those who are on limited incomes.
As has been pointed out by other hon. members, previous investigations and studies of food prices have been conducted in Canada. I would point out that in a relatively short time in terms of history, practically in one person's lifetime, there has been great change in farm practice and in the distribution and marketing of food. We have moved from subsistence to commercial farming.
There was a time when the consumer and the farmer met face to face over the sale of practically all farm products. Indeed, that can still happen here in Ottawa; consumers can still go to the Bytown market and buy flowers and vegetables directly from the growers. But that is the exception to the general rule. Over the years we have moved progressively to separate the consumer from the producer. This has proven to be a very expensive operation. It has cost both parties a great deal, and it is a continuing cost.
Recently the Manitoba department of agriculture began to publish the differences in retail and farm prices. A good example is eggs. A recent release states:
Traditionally, Winnipeg and Montreal have shared the dubious honour of having the largest spread between farm and retail prices for eggs, namely, 22 cents per dozen. By comparison, the average spread between farm and retail in Toronto has been 15 cents per dozen and in Regina 18 cents per dozen.
Nobody can really do very much about packaging an egg once the hen has laid it. About all that people in the chain from the producer to the consumer can do is wash it, put it in a carton and see that it gets on a shelf. For this the charge has been 22 cents a dozen in some Canadian cities. We should ask ourselves why this situation has taken place and why there is this wide difference in price. We often hear the story, "The consumer wants this kind of package. The consumer wants this done and that done." That really is not the whole story by a long shot. I have watched much of it unfold. Departments of agriculture

have played a role in it. University extension departments have played an important role; they have said, "There has to be better quality. We have to look after the quality of eggs, pork, broilers and turkeys."
Mr. Speaker, upon examination it will be found that at least 50 per cent of the changes that have taken place to ensure quality and conformity of the product were not to please the purchaser or producer but, rather, were an effort to develop a product that would move uniformly through the processes of packaging, evisceration or counter display in the stores. The changes were designed to facilitate these steps and make it easier for the processor or retailer to reap a larger profit with less trouble.

That was the reason for a good many of the changes. In many cases the benefit to the consumer was incidental, and in other cases it was the farmer who paid the price of the new regulations or controls. The dairy industry is a glaring example of this; it was so nearly run into the ground that the Canadian Dairy Commission had to be established in order to regulate it. If it were not for the commission, milk production would not have met the needs of the people of Canada. Indeed, even now cream producers have not been able to meet our needs because of these harsh regulations and for the last three years we have had to import butter, as we will again this year.
The other day the Minister of Agriculture said in the House that he faced this situation with equanimity, that our position is quite good. This country is one of the richest in agricultural resources of any western nation, yet the Minister of Agriculture is happy because we are not producing enough butter to look after our own people! This situation has developed at the expense of the farmer and the consumer and, in the process, control of some sectors of our agricultural industry has been turned over to multinational corporations whose concern for the consumer or producer is non-existent.

As we know, the Kraft Company has moved from thirty-second place to twenty-eighth place in the list of the largest corporations in North America. Last year its profits amounted to over $82 million. It operates in many countries of the world. Last summer the Standing Committee on Agriculture was trying to find out why at least one cheese factory, and perhaps more, could not get enough milk to manufacture cheese, and to this end had the dairy council appear before it. That factory had to close down, but at the same time the price of cheese to the consumer skyrocketed. This is part of the control process in our society with relation to the distribution of food.
A few years ago we had a surplus of grain, but not now. Some things should be realized when we tackle this question of food prices. The first is that the days of cheap land in Canada for agricultural purposes have just about come to an end, and the days of cheap labour are also coming to an end. This House can calculate what this will mean in relation to the question of cheap food. This year there is a world shortage of grain, especially rice. In some cases this
Food Prices Committee
has been the result of drought or flood in the rice producing regions, so we cannot continue to count on this bounty. Mr. Speaker, we will have to conserve our land and protect the people who farm it, otherwise the price of careless exploitation of the people or the land will be much higher than this society can afford.
If the standing committee which we are proposing can bring this one fact of life home to the Canadian people, then it will have accomplished something. If at the same time it can inform the consumers of Canada where the excess costs of food lie, that will be another very important contribution. Perhaps we can also cut down some of the barriers between consumer and producer both in terms of price and content. If we can do this, Mr. Speaker, we will have accomplished something.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had in this parliament to speak in any debate. I should like to make my opening remarks quite brief and incorporate all the nice things that have been said about you, just adding one of my own. Not only are you most fair, Sir, but I think what makes you an able Speaker is your ability to read human behaviour and your sense of humour which can keep the House on an even keel at times-even when the person speaking happens to be the member for Calgary North.
We are again debating the motion to set up a special committee dealing with food prices. The first paragraph of the motion asks:
That a special committee of this House be appointed to inquire into and make recommendations upon the trends in food prices in Canada and factors domestic and foreign which account for these trends-
Pursuant to another amendment passed, the other place has been deleted from membership on the committee. I intend to begin my remarks by saying that I propose at the end of my speech to move a further amendment which will reduce the number on this committee from 20 to 19. I intend to move that the figure "20" in the first line of the second paragraph be deleted and that the figure "19" be substituted therefor. My reason for moving the amendment is that in accordance with established prece-

January 22, 1973
Food Prices Committee
dent in this parliament there ought to be on all standing committees of the House eight government supporters, eight members from my party, two from the New Democratic Party and one from the other party, making a total of 19. I do not see why more than 19 should serve on this committee-this is the case with the supplementary estimate committee-and I think other hon. members will agree with me.
I shall now direct my remarks to the question of the price of food and other costs. Before doing so, I endorse fully the remarks made by the hon. member for North-umberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) regarding this committee. Certainly, I am prepared to see a committee of the House investigate high food prices. These prices have been going up and up. Between 1968 and 1972 they ran wild. We discussed this question during the election; it was one of the main election issues and I am happy to see that it has come before the House. But I am shocked, as a Member of this Parliament, that at this time, in view of the terrible shape the economy of this country is in, we should now be debating the setting up of a committee which at some time in the future will come up with some suggestions.
This reminds me of what the leader of the Creditiste party said; the government spent many millions of dollars on the B and B Commission to come to the conclusion that one part of the country speaks French and the other English. That commission cost $16 million. I say, when speaking about this committee, let us get down to brass tacks otherwise this committee is a sham. It is a farce, and shocks me. I was on the hustings, Mr. Speaker, and heard what many members of the NDP said about the government. They said it was doing nothing to cure inflation. According to some to them-and I agree-we are in worse shape now with regard to inflation than any other western nation. We have done nothing in the past four years to control it. Yet members of the NDP are now carrying this farce too far and behaving as if they were part of the government. That I find most shocking.
I should like the committee to look not only at food costs but at other costs, including shelter. The costs of shelter have risen by 60 per cent in the last short while. This affects drastically the wage earner, the pensioner, the man on fixed income, even the small businessman, because all need shelter. I do not think we need be concerned about food costs so much as about what our dollar will purchase. Money has become so inflated that people are not able to purchase as much food and shelter with their money as they could four years ago. That is the question we must study. What has happened to reduce the purchasing power of the dollar? In that regard we ought to discuss the government's position on taxation.
In the previous parliament-it is opportune to bring this to the attention of the House at this time because the committee should consider food costs and costs of shelter-a white paper on taxation was introduced. It was considered by a committee of this House for a considerable time. Then when the whole business was over, what was the result? The average, middle-income Canadian paid the highest amount he has ever paid in personal income tax. I do not have the figures before me relating to United States taxpayers; however, they pay less than the

taxpayers of this country. As I said, we pay higher taxes than ever. The government is taxing the farmer, the processor, the wholesaler, the retailer and, finally, the consumer. The few dollars left in his pay envelope will not stretch far enough so that he can afford the necessary groceries and shelter that his family needs.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
There is the problem. This government, by introducing its policy of high taxation in the last four years, has brought about the erosion of the dollar. It has aggravated the situation by permitting inflation which has been brought about through its taxation policies and its spending policies. I wish we could bring the estimates back before this House. This government has squandered millions of dollars. That, together with its policy of high taxation, has brought about inflation in the country. That is why we are debating the setting up of this committee, which I do not think will bring about any solution. By the time it reports, as hon. members know, inflation will have reached a new plateau and our people will be even shorter of cash. That is the situation.
I now want to talk about shelter costs and discuss what this government has done. Not long ago the then deputy prime minister of this country resigned. I am referring to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). He left the treasury benches because he could no longer go along with the economic policies of the government. That is why he resigned, Mr. Speaker. Today he is sitting on my side of the House. As I say, he resigned because he could no longer endorse economic policies which brought to this nation the highest rate of inflation among western nations.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
That was the main issue in the election. An article I hold in my hand is headlined, "Housing in Toronto is 'major social tragedy' ". The article reads.
ness than 4 per cent of Toronto wage earners can afford a new home, says a study by the Urban Development Institute which calls the city's housing situation a major social tragedy.
The study, released Wednesday, warns that 'unless drastic action is taken immediately, this situation will become more desperate.'
The institute's figures are based on a comparison of 1961 and 1971 incomes.
I am about to illustrate the magnitude of our inflationary problem. In 1961 when my party was in office an annual wage of $5,284 was enough to buy a house. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would lend a man earning such a salary enough money to obtain a mortgage, or would back a mortgage. So a man could buy a house if he earned a little over $5,000. In 1973, in Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Montreal or any other major centre, a person needs an income of $16,623 before he can qualify for a mortgage through CMHC. These are facts. This is inflation.
How did we reach this situation? In other words, why did the hon. member for Trinity resign from the government party? It will be remembered that the government had set up a task force on housing and then, when the hon. member brought in recommendations, refused to act

on them. At present the minister responsible for urban affairs is attending a conference. He said in a recent speech that the government will set aside $500 million for setting up a land bank. The acquisition will be spread over five years, which boils down to $100 million per year.
C. D. Howe once asked, "What's a million?". Perhaps I should ask this government, what is $100 million today in considering its land bank policy? If you took 640 acres in the north of Toronto and divided it up at ten lots to the acre, how much would you accomplish? Add another half section of land, making a total of 960 acres, divided that up, and how much would you accomplish? How much land do you think you can buy for $100 million surrounding one city, Toronto? Why, that amount would not be enough to buy the land for a Toronto development. So the whole thing is a sham.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am under the impression that we are discussing food prices. The hon. member has not yet mentioned food prices. Is it permissible to speak about housing and everything else, or should the hon. member be speaking about food prices?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I will answer that question, Mr. Speaker. I am talking about the cost of living. If the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) thinks the only problem in his constituency is the cost of food, and he is not concerned about shelter, he had better go back to Lake Centre and not to Regina, because I do not think those people will agree with him.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I want to continue with my thoughts about the cost of living. The problem today is that 60 per cent of the income earned by the average wage earner is needed to buy any form of shelter-and to give those people and their families any kind of dignity. That is the purpose of raising this question. I emphasize that a person must earn about $17,000 before he can qualify for a CMHC mortgage. That is three times greater than the salary required in 1961. Therefore with regard to how inflation is affecting the cost of houses, in the past ten years the situation has become three times worse because of this government's policies as far as inflation is concerned.
Let us look at another area. Let us go further west to Vancouver. I quote from the United Housing Foundation:
The cost of a housing lot in the greater Vancouver area has jumped $2,000 and in some cases $3,000 in one year-an 18 per cent increase. The average industrial wage earner is already hard put to it to find suitable housing for his family. Anyone on a limited income is in trouble now-the situation will get worse. Non-profit and co-operatively owned housing are an effective way of putting a lid on the spiralling costs of at least some of our housing stock-
At least this article makes certain recommendations. The housing situation is now tragic. People are unable to buy decent homes. They cannot buy a decent place for themselves and their families. Therefore I wish to make a recommendation. The motion should have been broad enough to cover the whole cost of living. If this committee
Food Prices Committee
is going to be of any help to Canadians, it should not only cover the price of food but the whole cost of living as far as Canadians are concerned.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Those on fixed pensions and incomes, with the exception of a few senior citizens who live in subsidized homes, are unable to purchase even the lowest priced house at the present time. Misery has been fanned everywhere by this government since 1968. A committee is now being established to look into the matter. Nothing whatsoever has been done since the last election in October, 1972. Perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) was correct: we see the same government, but the men are in different cabinet positions.
When the Minister of Finance told us what he thought of the new cabinet he gave a splendid answer, even though he was quoting somebody else. As far as this government is concerned, it is like somebody moving from one death chair to another on the Titanic. That is how bankrupt the government is. The Canadian people know that the government is bankrupt and has nothing to offer, and the quicker it goes to the people of Canada or gives up its job on the treasury benches, the better it will be for Canada.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Are you hungry, Eldon?

speechtext: I say to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) that I am not hungry but the people of Canada are hungry tonight. That is who is hungry.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: With the greatest respect, Sir, when talking about the price of housing surely it is relevant to discuss how to get it down to a fair price. Having said that, I now wish to turn to my amendment. As I said in my opening remarks, the proper number of members on this committee should be 19, the same as on the standing committee. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale):

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate very briefly. Indeed, I rise for only one purpose, to suggest a different figure for the number of members who should constitute this committee. As hon. members are aware, I raised this question in the House a few days ago in the hope that we could settle it by consultation among representatives of the various parties. However, since we did not achieve unanimous agreement on the point, the only way we can now resolve it is by putting the matter to the House.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel)]
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has made the assertion that all the standing committees of the House now consist of 19 members and therefore that is the proper number for this committee. May I make a slight correction to this assertion. It is not true that all standing committees number 19, or even 20 as the book says. There are two that have over 30 members each, and there are at least two that have 12 members. There are also two or three committees with memberships of 21 and 23. So there really is not anything sacred about the number 20 or the figure 19. The only reason that 19 has been chosen for a large number of the standing committees in this session is so that there can be equal representation by the two larger parties in this House of Commons.
However, when it comes to this committee we happen to think it is an important one. We are aware of all the time that has been lost since my leader during the election campaign demanded an immediate inquiry into the price of food. Nevertheless, it is better that it get started now than not be started at all.
We feel that if this inquiry is going to be made, the representation on the committee should be as close as possible to the proportionate representation of the parties in the House of Commons. If hon. members will do some arithmetic, they will find that out of 19 members we would be entitled to about two and a half, but we get only two.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
(Winnipeg North Centre): Mind you, our two may well be worth two and a half. If there are 25 members, the fractions work out a little more fairly, and this is one reason for our suggestion that this committee consist of 25 members. These 25 members should be made up as follows: ten Liberals; ten Progressive Conservatives-you cannot tell the difference between them, so we might as well have the same number each-three New Democrats and two representatives from the Social Credit party.
I said the other day that we would be glad to make it 25 or 30 members but that we are now prepared to settle for 25 on the understanding that they be divided in the way I have suggested. Therefore, we hope that the House will accept a subamendment to that effect.
Originally the government proposed a committee consisting of 30 members. We kicked off ten who were not exactly useful to the committee, so we can new split the difference between 20 and 30 and have the committee consist of 25 members. I hope the House will accept this proposal which, as I say, we tried to reach by consultation among the parties. As it turned out, three representatives agreed to 25 but the fourth did not.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought that when this committee was suggested with the number 20 as membership from the House of Commons, it was going to be a boondoggle participated in by members of this House, and at one point by members of the Senate. It is interesting that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) wants to increase the size of this boondoggle to 25. I would urge the members of the House, when the appropriate time comes, to restrict the number to 19 which seems more clearly to reflect the usefulness of the exercise.
At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to give notice that I will be moving a further amendment to the government motion before the House. This motion, in effect, will be to insert after the first paragraph, next after the word "Canada", the words "since 1967". The intention of the motion is to restrict the committee in its study of price and food trends to the years from 1967 to the present
Food Prices Committee
time. The motion is not in any way intended to restrict the effectiveness of the committee. Indeed, it is intended to increase effectiveness.
History has shown that we have had in this House a considerable number of committees examining the question of food prices. As so many speakers in this debate have pointed out, the most noteworthy committee in recent times was during the years 1966 and 1967. It seems to me that what the main motion before the House is doing is merely continuing that exercise which was terminated temporarily in 1967. It would assist whoever is chairing the committee and, indeed, the members and staff of the committee to focus on only immediate problems, those from 1967 to 1973.
Reference has been made in this House to a number of policy studies both by parliamentary committees and royal commissions. As early as 1935 there was a Commons committee on price spreads in the food industry. In 1948 there was another Commons committee, and in 1958 there was a royal commission. In 1967 there was a Commons committee. You can see how the cycle goes. In the mid-1950s royal commissions came into fashion. It seems to me the boondoggle was then transferred from members of this House to members of the civil service or those outside who happened to be friends of the government at a particular time. Then the boondoggle came back to this House in 1966-67. The studies have become a periodic ritual. But nothing was ever done.
There are many of us who will remember the activities of the 1966 committee as it travelled around the country holding hearings and then came back and held hearings in the city of Ottawa. During that time there were exposes on the front pages of many newspapers. There may have been some good work on the part of that committee, although that is sometimes difficult to discern.
I would honestly submit that we are engaged in the same old exercise which will have the same old results. It is high time the people of Canada had some new approach to problems in respect of food prices. We have not seen a new approach and I think the public is honestly looking for one. After all, this government does have other sources of information available to it. This committee is not going to uncover brand new questions for the first time and unearth facts, figures, views and concepts which will provide a startling and instant solution.
It is my understanding that there is, after all, a Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. This department apparently has officials who receive information from industry and a variety of sectors of the economy. Indeed, it was that department which sponsored the famous Bill C-256, the Competition Act, which was supposed to deal with combines and the exercise of a monopoly power in all sectors of the economy. This was an ill-conceived bill the likes of which this House had never seen. No doubt the new bill, if it ever comes, will be a significant improvement and more carefully drawn than the old one.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
It could not be worse.

January 22, 1973
Food Prices Committee

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Undoubtedly the new bill will be based on a wealth of information that many of us know the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has received during hearings and private meetings with the minister and members of his staff.
There has also been a prices and incomes commission in this country which apparently has done research on food prices. The members of this House and members of the public have not yet had the benefit of much of that research but it is hoped that it will be made available to members of the committee. Indeed, one would like to think there may be some wisdom emanating from that research on which the government might well have acted had it the will to act.
We also have in this country a Director of Investigation and Research under the Combines Investigation Act. I am sure members of this House are familiar with the powers of that gentleman and his staff, both his powers to investigate and the research carried on. One would hope that that sort of information could be available to the government and that it could act on it. One would hope the information will be available to members of the committee when they begin their investigation.
Finally, we have a body in this country called the Economic Council of Canada. It attempts to set economic goals and provide direction for the country on the frequent occasions when this government has not seen fit to do so. That council in its third annual report produced a document entitled "Prices, Productivity and Employment". That report and the background studies carried out pursuant to it provided useful documents for this government upon which it should have based a policy dealing with food prices. Again, these studies will be available to the committee. It represents part of the wealth of information available to this government upon which it should have acted.
With this wealth of information collected during the history of Commons committees, the shift to royal commissions and then back to Commons committees, and with the work of the Prices and Incomes Commission, the combines investigation branch, the officials of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Economic Council of Canada, we have almost exhausted the subject. It is very difficult to appreciate what useful purpose is to be served by yet another committee.
Lest we on this side of the House be understood as being completely negative in our approach, let me say that there are a few benefits which may result from this committee. I can think of the difficult position of the city dweller and his mystification about the very high and drastic increases in the price of food. I can understand his rather futile attempt to lay the blame at the doorstep of the most obvious and apparent person involved in the marketing of food, that is, the operator of the supermarket and the small, corner grocery store. One of the few useful purposes this committee might serve is to show the Canadian public that the problem is complex and that there is no single group to be blamed for the high price of food.
What the committee might do in its very detailed report, which we hope will eventually come out, is to set forth in skeleton form the structure of the food industry for the benefit of the Canadian people. In other words, the com-

mittee is an educational process. There are easier ways to educate the members of this House and the Canadian public, but if the committee has some value I suppose it should be viewed in this context.
Secondly, as the committee of 1966-67 pointed out, the very existence of a committee on food prices may have some short-term benefits in terms of a stabilization of food prices. It may be that with all the publicity given to the committee's hearings, housewives will attempt to shop more carefully and more selectively. This may be a shortterm benefit.
Thirdly, there may be some benefit flowing from the committee in the sense it will encourage participants in the food industry to try harder to lower prices. One of the great revelations of the 1966-67 committee was the extent of monopoly power and control in the food industry. It may be that just the publicity given committee hearings will once again result in some voluntary price reductions by participants in the food industry, whether they be wholesalers, retailers or producers. They may choose to revise their particular structural organizations which will result in freer competition and lower prices for food.
All these are merely short-term, temporary solutions with marginal benefits at best. Certainly they are marginal when one compares them with the time to be invested by the committee members and the expense and the attention required of a large number of members of this House and others in what may prove to be a futile exercise.
As the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) has indicated, we will co-operate in the conduct of the proceedings of this committee. I am not sure it will remedy the mystery which is still in the minds of a great many people throughout this country as to where the blame lies. But it will do one thing. It will prove more than ever that in recent years there is one party which could have done something about food prices but has not. That is the government. The government has not acted, and the Canadian people are going to realize that.
Therefore, to expedite the work of the committee I should like to formally move my amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald). I move:
That the motion be amended by inserting in the first paragraph thereof, next after the word "Canada", the words "since 1967".
There is one additional matter I would raise in the context of this debate. It is the question of comparing food prices in the major cities in Canada with food prices in certain major cities of the country to the south of us. I raise this more as a question than as a matter of providing any definitive facts or answers. I am referring to a survey conducted by the Montreal Star which contains a comparison of the price of a typical grocery basket purchased by an average family in Canada in the month of June, 1972, and by an average family in the United States in the same period. Significantly, the Canadian cities proposed for this survey were Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver. The comparison was with the United States cities of New York, Chicago, St. Louis and San Francisco. One might say that this selection of cities represents a fair sampling of cities in the case of each country.
January 22, 1973

In all four Canadian cities the price of the average basket of groceries was significantly higher than the price in the United States cities. In my city of Toronto the price was $32.03 for the grocery basket selected, while the price for a similar grocery basket in the so-called expensive city of New York was $28.67. I would hope that the significant variations in food prices for those living north of the border in comparison to those living south of the border might become one of the major subjects of investigation by members of the committee. The answer might possibly be in the broader context of the special controls which might be instituted pursuant to a foreign investment policy by this or other governments, but I believe it is a question which should be dealt with.

I found it a little surprising that members of the party to my right, for the first time in that party's history-and I noted that the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was away that day; perhaps it was accidental, perhaps it was not-should have come before the House and proposed the removal of the Senate from this committee. Cynicism?
The second amendment they brought before us was that the serious study made of the increase in food prices be completed after a mere three months. Anyone with an ounce of brains and two ounces of political commitment to this important issue should know that such an amendment is completely idiotic.
Finally, a new member of the House-I do not criticize him particularly since he is acting for that dishevelled crowd on my right-presented an amendment which provides that we cannot look at what causes rising food prices for a period antedating 1967. Quite apart from that-perhaps a relevant political point of a cheap nature which they are trying to make- there is also the important intellectual and academic fact that you cannot talk about trends in food pricing, you cannot talk about the price-making policies of the large food chains, you cannot talk about anything of a serious nature in pricing in the economy if you look only at a three or four-year trend. What I am saying on this point is that every amendment brought by the Conservative party shows that they do not take the increase in food prices

speechtext:
In my concluding comments I want to suggest as precisely as I can some important issues that this committee might consider and deal with in a concrete way, issues that could have an effect, not in six months perhaps but within a year in terms of a permanent, long-range pricing policy on food in Canada. That is what this kind of committee should deal with in part. In part, also, it should be making early recommendations to deal with the immediate crisis. That is why we have an amendment calling for an interim report to be presented to the House in two months. But the main thrust of the committee's work should be concerned with a recommendation to keep food prices in Canada down in the long run so that Canadians with an average income, and in particular those who are poor, can afford to eat well.
What can this committee do in a serious way that the Conservative party would not call boondoggling? First of all, it can find out who is getting the food dollar, the farmer or the middleman. We know some facts on this already. We know that in 1949, for example, the farmer was getting 57 cents of every dollar spent on food. In 1972, last year, his share had dropped to 38 cents. I have another statistic on the share that the farmer is getting and I think it should be brought before the House since I come from an urban constituency and think it is very important indeed to make it quite clear that farmers in Canada are by no means getting their share of the food dollar, at least on the basis of the preliminary evidence.
The net income of farmers from their farm operations declined in the last three-year period, when the average income of other Canadians was going up, from 1968 to 1971 by 8 per cent. In addition, those of us who will be working in the committee in a serious way might find out what real impact the packaging industry has on food prices, what real impact advertising has on the share of the dollar spent, and how it contributes to the rising cost of food. These are serious questions that have to be looked at in a serious way and, if I may say so, must be examined by our party also. We do not pretend to have all the answers.

resources. In Oshawa and Hamilton the organized trade union movement played an important part in their initial financing. I would like the committee to consider what role federal financing might play in the spread of direct charge co-ops across the country, as one means of keeping down food prices.
The third item the committee might consider is why there are significant disparities in food costs between one region of Canada and another. Just the other day one of the ministers of the British Columbia government was in town and some of us had a discussion with him. Just because we were debating this subject he mentioned that there was a small town north of the city of Vancouver where food prices were 30 per cent higher than in Vancouver. What are the reasons for this? Are there just two or three stores in that town that effectively eliminate competition? I do not immediately know the answer, but it is an important question.
This is also a problem within big cities. Studies have been conducted in Canada, and more particularly in the United States, which show that the large supermarkets charge poor people the most for their products. In the ghetto areas of large cities the costs of basic commodities such as meat, milk and bread are frequently higher than they are in upper-income suburbs. One of the reasons for this is that the mobility of lower-income citizens is substantially less than the more affluent, and thus stores in those areas have a captive market and, if you like, can gouge poor people. If that is the case, I for one think it should be stopped.

A study that seriously looks at food prices must examine that question. The committee might come up with a particular solution-in this case it might be an increase in pensions-or it might be selective price control over certain essential commodities to ensure that all Canadians, regardless of income, are assured of a sound nutritional diet.
Fifthly, I suggest that the committee ought to summon before it the heads of large supermarkets. In this respect I give full credit to the government of the United States of which, on other grounds, I am frequently quite critical. The congressional system, in terms of public hearings, is simply light years ahead of the parliament of Canada. In the United States, when they look at such matters as automobile prices or food prices committees are given effective powers to call witnesses before them and those witnesses must provide the information requested.
I for one would like to get the heads of Loblaws, IGA, Steinberg's, Canadian Safeway and Dominion Stores before the committee to explain their profits.
